input:
Centrifugal pumps are among the most widely used machines in process plants, and understanding how their performance changes when the rotational speed is varied is a crucial part of pump engineering. The well-known affinity laws provide a convenient and powerful framework for describing exactly this behaviour, and they can be summarised in terms of three simple proportionalities that relate flow, head and power to speed.

Firstly, the flow delivered by the pump is directly proportional to the speed, since each revolution of the impeller displaces essentially the same volume of liquid, which means that doubling the speed will, in effect, double the flow. Secondly, the head developed by the pump is proportional to the square of the speed, because the head follows the square of the impeller tip speed, which itself increases in direct proportion to the rotational speed, so that doubling the speed leads to four times the head. Thirdly, the power is proportional to the cube of the speed, reflecting the combined effect of the flow and head dependencies acting together.

A simple worked check illustrates the power relationship nicely: when the speed is doubled, the flow doubles and the head increases fourfold, and the power therefore increases by a factor of 8. It is worth noting that the same factor of 8 emerges directly from the cube of the speed ratio. Overall, the affinity laws offer an elegant and remarkably useful way of estimating pump performance at off-design speeds, although it should be borne in mind that they rely on the assumption of geometric similarity between the operating points and on the efficiency remaining broadly unchanged between them, so the estimates they provide should be treated as approximations in practice.
target:
This tutorial explains the pump affinity laws: the relations that carry the performance of a centrifugal pump from one rotational speed to another. The outcome is three proportionalities and one worked check. Doubling the speed multiplies the power by 8, and the passage shows where that factor comes from.

Flow varies in direct proportion to speed. Each revolution of the impeller displaces a fixed volume of liquid, so the volume delivered in a given time rises in step with the number of revolutions in that time. Twice the speed gives twice the flow, provided the flow pattern inside the impeller passages stays geometrically similar, so that the volume displaced by each revolution does not itself change with speed.

Head varies with the square of the speed. The head a centrifugal stage develops follows the square of the impeller tip speed, and the tip speed rises in direct proportion to the rotational speed. Doubling the speed therefore gives four times the head, because the quantity that sets the head has itself doubled and the head follows its square.

Power varies with the cube of the speed. Power is the product of flow and head for a liquid of given density at a given efficiency: flow contributes one factor of speed, head contributes two, and the product carries all three. The worked check applies the cube law to a doubled speed. The flow doubles and the head quadruples, and the power rises by the product of those two factors, which is a factor of 8.

The three proportionalities rest on geometric similarity between the two operating points being compared. Where the flow pattern changes with speed, or where the efficiency at the new speed differs from the efficiency at the old, the laws hold only as approximations, and a performance figure carried from one speed to another by these relations carries that approximation with it.
